title: Hoppin' John
subtitle: Black-eyed peas and rice with ham hock, a New Year tradition
excerpt: Hoppin' John is a Southern dish of dried black-eyed peas simmered with a smoked ham hock and then cooked together with rice. Eating it on New Year's Day is said to bring good luck throughout the year. The dish is simple, filling, and takes about 90 minutes. The pot liquor is the sauce.
sourceNotes: Southern American culinary tradition, particularly South Carolina and the Lowcountry. Hoppin' John is documented as a New Year's Day dish in Edna Lewis, The Taste of Country Cooking (1976). Its West African origins are evident in the combination of black-eyed peas and rice, a pairing central to West African cooking.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze without the rice for up to 3 months. Add freshly cooked rice when reheating.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The beans can be cooked a day ahead. Rice is best made fresh.

content.text: Hoppin' John is dried black-eyed peas simmered with a smoked ham hock until tender, then mixed with long-grain rice and some of the cooking liquid. The beans absorb the smokiness of the pork as they cook. The whole dish is seasoned simply: the flavour comes from the ham and the peas themselves.

items.prepNote: dried, soaked overnight in cold water

content.text: Drain and rinse the soaked {{black-eyed-beans}} of black-eyed peas. Put them in the Dutch oven with the {{ham-hock}} ham hock, {{onion}} onion, {{celery}} celery, {{garlic}} of garlic, and {{bay-leaves}} of bay. Cover with cold water by 5 cm. Bring to a boil, skim any foam, then reduce to a steady simmer. Cook uncovered for 1 to 1.5 hours until the peas are completely tender.
Lift out the ham hock. Pull the meat from the bone, shred it, and return to the pot. Remove the bay leaves. Season with salt and pepper. The pot liquid should be a flavourful broth.

Cook {{long-grain-rice}} of rice separately. Serve the peas over or alongside the rice, spooning the pot liquor over generously. Scatter with {{spring-onion}} spring onions. Hot sauce is on the table.

items.cause: Old beans, or salt added too early.
items.fix: Do not add salt until the beans are tender. Old dried peas take significantly longer.

items.cause: Ham hock released a lot of salt.
items.fix: Taste before adding any seasoning. The ham hock seasons the dish throughout the cook.

content.text: The peas can be cooked with the rice in the traditional one-pot method: after the peas are tender, add the rice and enough cooking liquid to cook it. Collard greens served alongside, often called the Lowcountry New Year plate, complete the meal.

Hoppin' John is one of the most widely eaten New Year's Day dishes in the American South. The tradition of eating black-eyed peas for luck on New Year's Day goes back to at least the Civil War era and is thought to have West African origins. The peas represent coins, and the collard greens eaten alongside represent paper money.
